For the circle this component is zero everywhere, because the normal is parallel to the radius and the vector perpendicular to it. For the rectangle the normal of the face \(y = a\) is parallel to the axis \(y\), and the vector \(G\alpha(-z, y)\) has there the component \(-G\alpha z\). The corner with two components is the extreme case: the stress vector has length \(8{,}39\) MPa, at the place where all the shear stress must be zero.

So what Duleau noticed shows up. For the circle the shear vector at the edge is along the edge. For the rectangle it must be just so, because every free surface requires it (figure 16.8), and at the corner, where it must not point across either of the two faces, even zero. The field of the circle cannot do this. The assumptions of elementary strength of materials are therefore not slightly inexact for the rectangle, they fail the boundary condition. The next section therefore extends the displacement: we add to it a displacement along the axis, \(u_{\mathrm{x}} \ne 0\), which makes the sections bulge, and look for the \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) that satisfies the boundary condition.

16.2 Warping function (funkcija zvitja)

The previous section showed that the field of the circle fails on the \(20 \times 40\) mm strip: on the free long face it leaves a stress of \(7{,}50\) MPa, and at the corner a stress of \(8{,}39\) MPa where it must be zero (lemma 16.14). The field assumed that the section stays plane, that is, that all its points move only in the plane of the section. If this is not true, then besides turning about the axis a point of the section must also move along the axis. How much, and how to compute it for every section, not only for a rectangle, is the question of this section.

From history

That the sections of a twisted bar do not stay plane was first noticed by Cauchy. Applying the general equations of elasticity to rectangular bars, he found a satisfactory solution for a narrow rectangle and showed that the sections of a twisted bar in general do not stay plane but bulge (TIMO, PDF p. 118). LOVE says that his result was not correct, but that it is historically important because he recognized that the normal sections do not remain plane (LOVE, PDF p. 36). No year for Cauchy's work is given on these pages. Attempts to use the assumption of plane sections for shafts of other shapes did not agree with experiments (TIMO, PDF p. 207). For this reason Saint-Venant assumed only a rotation of the section in its own plane and added the warping as an unknown that the equations of elasticity determine (TIMO, PDF p. 207). This is the semi-inverse method (definition 11.11), which chapter 11 presented together with Saint-Venant's treatise. This section carries it through to the end. The bulge he speaks of is shown by the figure in this section.

The semi-inverse method is a proposal, and the field equations tell whether the proposal holds. We propose that every section at \(x\) rotates about the origin \(O\) by the angle \(\alpha x\), as in equation (16.2), and that at the same time its points move along the axis by a length that depends only on the place \((y, z)\) in the section and not on \(x\). Why not on \(x\)? Every piece of the prism with the same section and length carries the same moment (section 16.1) and therefore deforms in the same way. Why proportional to \(\alpha\)? The problem is linear and \(\alpha\) is the only parameter of the load, so every displacement is a multiple of it.

Let us draw what we propose (figure 16.15). On the left is the section \(20 \times 40\) mm viewed along the axis \(x\), with the coordinate axes \(y\) and \(z\) and the origin \(O\). The point \(P\) is the corner with the coordinates \(y = a = 10\) mm and \(z = b = 20\) mm. As before, \(P\) moves in the plane of the section by the vector \(\vek d\), perpendicular to \(OP\). On the right is the view from the side, with the axes \(x\) and \(z\). The grey vertical line is the section before loading, drawn at one place \(x\). After loading the points of the face \(y = a\) move along the axis: at \(z = 0\) not at all, above in the direction \(+x\), below in the direction \(-x\), at the corner \(z = b\) by \(0{,}832\) \(\mu\)m and at most \(0{,}953\) \(\mu\)m at \(z = 16{,}6\) mm, at \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m. The points of the face \(y = -a\) move in the opposite direction, so the section does not rotate as a rigid body but bulges like a saddle. The length of the arrow between the grey line and the curve at \(z = 15\) mm is the displacement \(\alpha\psi\) of that point, \(0{,}934\) \(\mu\)m. The displacements are drawn \(12\,600\) times larger than in reality, and the curves are computed with the series of section 16.5 and serve here only as a view of what we are looking for.

The word warping translates the Slovenian zvitje. Let us write the proposal as a definition.

Definition 16.15 Warping function (funkcija zvitja)

Let a prism with section \(S\) be uniformly twisted (definition 16.1) with the twist per unit length \(\alpha \ne 0\). The displacement of the point \((x, y, z)\), the rotation about the axis and the displacement along it, has the form

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha\,\psi(y, z) , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = -\alpha\,x\,z , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = \alpha\,x\,y , \tag{16.19}\]

where \(\psi : S \to \mathbb{R}\) is a twice continuously differentiable function on an open set that contains \(S\). We call the function \(\psi\) the warping function (funkcija zvitja), and measure its values in mm\(^2\).

Explanation

The unit is such that \(\alpha\psi\) is a length: \(\alpha\) is in rad/mm (rad is a number without a unit) and \(\psi\) in mm\(^2\). The value \(\alpha\psi(y, z)\) is the displacement of the point of the section along the axis, which the arrow \(\alpha\psi\) on the right half of figure 16.15 shows. For the circle \(\psi = 0\) (section 16.1). The letter \(\psi\) has several meanings in the book: a trial function in chapter 6 and a shape function in chapter 7. In this chapter it means only the warping function.

Source: SADD section 9.3 (PDF pp. 246 and 247): the in-plane displacement is a rigid rotation about the center of twist \(O\), where \(u = v = 0\), the rotation is a linear function of the axial coordinate, and the displacement along the axis, which SADD calls \(w\), is an unknown function of the coordinates in the section only (SADD (9.3.3)). SADD has the axis \(z\) along the bar, we have the axis \(x\), its \(w(x, y)\) is our \(\alpha\psi(y, z)\) and its \(\alpha\) is our \(\alpha\). The name warping function with the symbol \(\psi\) and the definition are ours.

What does the displacement (16.19) do to the strains? The first part, \((0, -\alpha xz, \alpha xy)\), is the rotation of the section about \(O\) by the angle \(\alpha x\) that we already know, and the second part, \((\alpha\psi, 0, 0)\), is a displacement that has only a component along the axis and depends only on the place in the section. Chapter 11 called this form, with a component along the axis, the antiplane state and announced it as the setting of torsion. Let us draw them on a small square of material (figure 16.16) and compute the strains of both parts together.

On the left is the square in the plane \(xy\) at the point \((y, z)\) with sides \(\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\mathrm{d}y\). The twist tilts the side \(\mathrm{d}x\) toward the axis \(y\) by the angle \(-\alpha z\), because \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -\alpha x z\). The warping tilts the side \(\mathrm{d}y\) toward the axis \(x\) by the angle \(\alpha\psi_{\mathrm{y}}\), because \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha\psi\) and the displacement along the axis varies with \(y\). The right angle between the sides therefore changes by the shear angle, the sum of the two tilts. On the right is the square in the plane \(yz\): the twist only rotates it, the sides stay equally long and perpendicular, so there is no deformation in this plane.

Lemma 16.16 Strains in torsion (deformacije pri torziji)

Let the displacement have the form (16.19). Then at every point of the prism, as the small square shows,

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0 , \qquad \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z) , \qquad \gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y) , \tag{16.20}\]

where \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}}\) mean \(\partial\psi/\partial y\) and \(\partial\psi/\partial z\). The strains depend only on \((y, z)\) and not on \(x\). By Hooke's law (theorem 3.19) the only nonzero stresses are

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z) , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y) . \tag{16.21}\]
Idea

Every term is a derivative of a product in which one factor is \(x\) or does not depend on the variable we differentiate by. In the figure these are the twist, which only rotates the square, and the tilt due to \(\psi\).

Proof
  1. By definition 1.121, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = \alpha\,\partial\psi/\partial x = 0\), because \(\psi\) does not depend on \(x\). Similarly \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = -\alpha x\,\partial z/\partial y = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = 0\). The sides of the square do not get longer.
  2. \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial y) = \tfrac12(-\alpha x + \alpha x) = 0\). The square in the plane \(yz\) only rotates.
  3. \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x) = \tfrac12\alpha(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z)\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x) = \tfrac12\alpha(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y)\). The shear strains are by convention twice these. This is the shear angle, the sum of the tilt due to warping and of the twist.
  4. The trace of the strain is zero by step 1, so by Hooke's law \(\ten\sigma = 2G\,\ten\varepsilon\). Only the components with the indices \(xy\) and \(xz\) are nonzero (and the symmetric \(yx\), \(zx\) by theorem 2.41). Only the shear strain is nonzero, so the stress is shear only.

Source: SADD section 9.3.1, equations (9.3.4) and (9.3.5) (PDF p. 247): from the displacement (9.3.3) it obtains the same two shear strains. The split into rotation and antiplane part is ours.

Let us see what this means for our strip, the right half of figure 16.15. At the middle of the long face, at the point \((a, 0)\), the rotation alone gives the stress \(G\alpha\,(-z, y) = (0,\ G\alpha a)\), that is \(6{,}83\) MPa at \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m and the true \(\alpha = 9{,}064 \cdot 10^{-6}\) rad/mm, which section 16.5 computes for the strip. Section 16.1 computed \(\alpha\) with the polar moment \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\), got a smaller \(\alpha\) and therefore only \(3{,}75\) MPa there. The true stress \(12{,}71\) MPa, which section 16.5 computes, we obtain only with the warping: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 1{,}686 \cdot 10^{-4}\). The stress there is tangent to the face \(y = a\), as the free face demands, and almost twice as large as the rotation alone would give.

Did we overlook something in the rotation? The field (16.19) is the linear form of the true rotation and neglects \(R(1 - \cos\varphi)\) (section 16.1). For the strip \(20 \times 40\) mm and the length \(1\) m the corner is \(22{,}36\) mm from the axis. The ratio \((1 - \cos\varphi)/\sin\varphi = \tan(\varphi/2)\) tells by what fraction of its displacement the corner at the end lies off compared with the true rotation. At \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m, \(\varphi(L) = 0{,}00906\) rad, this is \(0{,}453\,\%\), and at \(500\) N m, \(\varphi(L) = 0{,}0906\) rad, it is \(4{,}53\,\%\). This error concerns the position of the points, not the stresses. The stresses depend on the strains, which at \(50\) N m are at most \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 1{,}686 \cdot 10^{-4}\). At \(500\) N m, however, the model fails earlier because of the material: the largest shear stress of the strip is \(127{,}1\) MPa, above the shear yield stress \(110\) MPa by the Tresca condition (section 16.5), and the strip is no longer linearly elastic there. For this reason we took \(50\) N m for the strip.

Now we look for \(\psi\). Let us draw what the prism demands (figure 16.17). The body is a prism with the section \(S\) and the length \(L\). The field equations must hold in it, which is the first demand. The lateral surface is free, so the stress vector there is zero, which is the second demand. On the end section the stress vector is \((0, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\), which gives a resultant of zero and the moment \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is the third demand. Let us begin with the boundary.

Let us draw the free lateral surface on a section that we can test (figure 16.18). For the boundary take an ellipse with the semi-axes \(10\) mm along \(y\) and \(20\) mm along \(z\), drawn with the axes and the origin \(O\), and on it the point \(B\) with the coordinates \(y = 8{,}660\) mm and \(z = 10{,}000\) mm. There the outward normal \(\vek n\) has the components \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0{,}9608\) and \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0{,}2774\), and the tangent is perpendicular to it. We divide the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) by \(G\alpha\) to get a vector in mm, and write it as \(\vek s = (\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z,\ \psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y)\). It is the sum of two parts: the rotation vector \(\vek q = (-z, y)\) with the components \(-10{,}000\) mm and \(8{,}660\) mm, which is perpendicular to \(OB\) and so tangent to the circle about \(O\) through \(B\) of radius \(|OB| = 13.23\) mm, and the gradient \(\nabla\psi = (\psi_{\mathrm{y}}, \psi_{\mathrm{z}})\). For \(\psi = 0{,}6\,yz\), a function that section 16.3 finds for the ellipse, \(\nabla\psi\) has the components \(6{,}000\) mm and \(5{,}196\) mm. Their sum is the stress vector \(\vek s\) with the components \(-4{,}000\) mm and \(13{,}856\) mm. The free face cannot carry a force, so \(\vek s\) must be tangent to the boundary, that is perpendicular to \(\vek n\): indeed \(\vek q \cdot \vek n = -7{,}206\) and \(\nabla\psi \cdot \vek n = 7{,}206\), and the sum \(\vek s \cdot \vek n\) is zero. With \(\psi = 0\) the sum would be \(\vek q\) alone and \(\vek s \cdot \vek n = -7{,}206 \ne 0\). So the condition becomes an equation for the normal derivative of \(\psi\) on the boundary.

For the theorem we also need the divergence theorem in the plane, which we obtain from the theorem for the prism. Let us draw it (figure 16.19). On the right is the prism with its end faces and mantle, on the left the section \(S\) with its boundary, the outward normal \(\vek n\) and the field \(\vek v\), which does not depend on \(x\).

Lemma 16.17 Divergence theorem in the section (izrek o divergenci v prerezu)

Let \(S\) be a section for which the prism \(S \times [0, \ell]\) is a body from corollary 4.68, cut so that every outer piece of the lateral surface is described by \((t, x) \mapsto (x, \gamma(t))\) for \(t \in [t_0, t_1]\) and \(x \in [0, \ell]\). Here \(\gamma = (\gamma_{\mathrm{y}}, \gamma_{\mathrm{z}})\) is an arc of the boundary \(\partial S\), continuously differentiable with \(\gamma'(t) \ne \vek 0\). This holds for all sections in this chapter: the circle, the annulus (for example four curved boxes in cylindrical coordinates, definition 4.65), the ellipse, the triangle, the rectangle. The boundary \(\partial S\) has the outward normal \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\). Let \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) be a field continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\). Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{S}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint_{\partial \mathrm{S}} \big( v_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}s , \tag{16.22}\]

where the integral of a function \(f\) over the boundary is the sum of the integrals over its arcs,

\[\oint_{\partial \mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}s = \sum_{\gamma} \int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1} f\big(\gamma(t)\big)\,|\gamma'(t)|\,\mathrm{d}t .\]

For \(f = 1\) this is the length of the boundary by definition 8.5, so we call \(s\) the arc length of the boundary.

Proof
  1. The field \((0, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) does not depend on \(x\) and is continuously differentiable. Its divergence is the sum in the expression on the left. The field lies in the plane of the section.
  2. By corollary 4.68 the integral of the divergence over the prism equals the flux through its surface. The integral over the prism is \(\ell\) times the integral over the section, because the function does not depend on \(x\). The surface of the prism is the end faces and mantle.
  3. On both end faces the normal is \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), so \((0, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\cdot\vek n = 0\). A piece of the lateral surface described by \(\vek r(t, x) = (x, \gamma_{\mathrm{y}}(t), \gamma_{\mathrm{z}}(t))\) has the derivatives \(\partial\vek r/\partial t = (0, \gamma_{\mathrm{y}}', \gamma_{\mathrm{z}}')\) and \(\partial\vek r/\partial x = (1, 0, 0)\), so its surface vector is \(\pm(0, \gamma_{\mathrm{z}}', -\gamma_{\mathrm{y}}')\), of length \(|\gamma'(t)|\). It points outward, so it equals \(|\gamma'(t)|\,(0, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\). The field does not depend on \(x\), so by definition 4.65 the flux through this piece is \(\int_0^\ell\!\int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1}(v_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}})\,|\gamma'(t)|\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}x = \ell\int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1}(v_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}})\,|\gamma'(t)|\,\mathrm{d}t\). The sum over all pieces of the lateral surface is \(\ell\oint(v_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s\). The end faces contribute nothing, the mantle gives the flux through the boundary.
  4. Cancel \(\ell\). We cancel the length of the prism.

Source: The plane form of the divergence theorem is in SADD (1.8.11) (PDF p. 28), which it uses in (9.3.15) and (9.3.17) (PDF p. 250). The derivation from corollary 4.68 with a prism is not from the source.

Now we have everything for the theorem. It joins the three demands of figure 16.17: the field equation for \(\psi\) in the body, the condition on the boundary, and the forces at the ends.

Theorem 16.18 Saint-Venant torsion (Saint-Venantova torzija)

Let \(S\) be a bounded section for which lemma 16.17 holds and whose interior is connected. Let \(\psi\) be twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\) (for a rectangle this fails at the corners, section 16.5), and let \(\alpha \ne 0\). Let the material be as in theorems 11.6 and 11.4. Let us write two conditions for \(\psi\), the equation in the body and the condition on the free surface:

\[\nabla^2\psi = \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial z^2} = 0 \quad \text{in } S , \qquad \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial n} = \psi_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \psi_{\mathrm{z}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} = z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}} \quad \text{on } \partial S . \tag{16.23}\]

For the displacement (16.19) the following holds:

  1. It satisfies the Navier-Lamé equations (theorem 11.6) with zero body force exactly when the first equation \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\) holds. This is the demand for the body.
  2. The lateral surface is free exactly when the second condition holds, the boundary condition for \(\partial\psi/\partial n\). This is the demand for the lateral surface.
  3. If both conditions hold, the resultant force on every end section is zero, and the moment about the axis \(x\) is On the end these are the resultant and the moment.
    \[M_{\mathrm{x}} = G\,J\,\alpha , \qquad J = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \big( y^2 + z^2 + y\,\psi_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,\psi_{\mathrm{y}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{16.24}\]
  4. This field is, up to a small rigid displacement, the only one with such surface forces on the whole surface of the prism. The surface forces act on the lateral surface and the end. The number \(J\) is called the torsion constant (torzijska konstanta), \(GJ\) the torsional rigidity (torzijska togost), \(J\) in mm\(^4\).
Idea

We check everything that the boundary value problem demands, as for the circle. The free surface brings a condition on the boundary, and the resultant and the moment we get with the divergence theorem in the plane. Uniqueness is a theorem of chapter 11. The three demands are the body, lateral surface and end.

Proof
  1. From equation (16.19), \(\nabla^2u_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha(\psi_{\mathrm{yy}} + \psi_{\mathrm{zz}})\), \(\nabla^2u_{\mathrm{y}} = \nabla^2u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) (the components are linear in every variable), and \(\operatorname{div}\vek u = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = 0 + 0 + 0\). By theorem 11.6 and \(\mu = G\) (definition 3.18) the left side of equation (11.3) equals \((G\alpha\,\nabla^2\psi,\ 0,\ 0)\), so the equation holds exactly when \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\). This is point 1.
  2. On the lateral surface the normal is \(\vek n = (0, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\). By Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.26), \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(t_{\mathrm{y}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}n_{\mathrm{z}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) and \(t_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), because by lemma 16.16 all other stresses are zero. The component \(t_{\mathrm{x}}\) is zero exactly when \(G\alpha(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \psi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}} - zn_{\mathrm{y}} + yn_{\mathrm{z}}) = 0\), and since \(G\alpha \ne 0\) this is \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \psi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = zn_{\mathrm{y}} - yn_{\mathrm{z}}\). This is point 2.
  3. Let (16.23) hold. On the end section at \(x = L\) with the normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) the stress vector is \(\vek t = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}) = (0, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) by theorem 2.41. By equation (16.21), \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial y + \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial z = G\alpha\,\nabla^2\psi = 0\).
  4. The field \(\vek v = (y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}},\ y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) is continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\) and has the divergence \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} + y\,(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial y + \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial z) = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) by step 3. By lemma 16.17, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint y\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\), since the expression in the parentheses is zero on the boundary (step 2). Likewise with the field \((z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}},\ z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) for \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\). The force in the direction \(x\) is zero because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\). So the resultant is zero. This shows that the resultant on the end is zero.
  5. Because of \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and the zero resultant, the moments about the axes \(y\) and \(z\), \(\int(z\,t_{\mathrm{x}} - L\,t_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}A = -L\int\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\) and \(\int(L\,t_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,t_{\mathrm{x}})\,\mathrm{d}A = L\int\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), are zero. The moment about the axis \(x\) is \(\int(y\,t_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,t_{\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}A = \int(y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} - z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\,\mathrm{d}A = G\alpha\int(y\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y^2 - z\psi_{\mathrm{y}} + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A = G\alpha J\). At \(x = 0\) the normal is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the resultant and the moment are opposite. This is point 3. The moment on the end is given by the moment.
  6. The forces on the whole surface are thus given and there is no body force. Let \(\tilde{\vek u}\) be another field with the same surface forces. By theorem 11.4, point 2, the difference \(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) is a small rigid displacement. This is point 4. The surface forces on the lateral surface and the end are thus given.
Explanation

The torsion constant \(J\) replaces the polar moment \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) of the circle. Example (figure 16.22): for the rectangle \(20 \times 40\) mm, \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\) and \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 133\,333\) mm\(^4\) (section 16.5). The product \(GJ\) is what chapter 12 took as a model in equation (12.16), and chapter 13 took \(GI_{\mathrm{p}}\) for the circle in equation (13.20). The theorem proves the equation for every section for which the function \(\psi\) that solves the conditions (16.23) is twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\): for the circle and the annulus (\(\psi = 0\)) and for the ellipse (\(\psi = 0{,}6\,yz\) for the semi-axes \(10\) and \(20\) mm, section 16.3). The rectangle has corners where \(\psi\) does not meet this condition (section 16.5). The proof would need cutting out small squares around the corners and a limit, which we do not carry out here, so for the rectangle the theorem is not proved here. The numbers for the strip in this section are computed with the series of section 16.5. The ends are loaded only with the distribution \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) of equation (16.21). A different loading of the end with the same moment differs, by Saint-Venant's principle (section 11.11, stated there and not proved), only near the end. The solution is thus exact for this loading, and for others it holds far from the ends.

Source: SADD section 9.3.2, equations (9.3.19) to (9.3.24) (PDF p. 251): \(\nabla^2 w = 0\) in the section, the condition on the normal derivative on the boundary, \(T = \alpha\mu J\) with \(J\) defined as an integral over the section. The proof with the Navier-Lamé equations, the divergence theorem and uniqueness is ours. SADD's \(T\) is our \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), its \(J\) is our \(GJ\).

We wrote the boundary so that the derivative of the function \(\psi\) along the normal is known and the value is not. Such problems have an unusual property: they cannot be solved for every right-hand side.

Let us draw this (figure 16.20). On the left is the circle with the radius \(20\) mm, and on its boundary we would like \(\partial\psi/\partial n = 10\) mm everywhere, which the orange arrows with the datum \(g = 10\) show, all outward. Since \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\), the field \(\nabla\psi\) has neither a source nor a sink in the interior, so as much as flows out would also have to flow in. The total outflow through the boundary would be \(2\pi \cdot 20 \cdot 10 = 1256{,}6\) mm\(^2\), and there is no inflow anywhere. Such a \(\psi\) does not exist. On the right is the rectangle \(20 \times 40\) mm and the arrows on its boundary show the right-hand side of the torsion condition, \(g = z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\). Where \(g > 0\), an orange arrow points out, where \(g < 0\), a blue one points in. On the face \(y = a\) we have \(g = z\): for \(z > 0\) the arrows point out, for \(z < 0\) in, and the sum over this face is zero. On the face \(z = b\) we have \(g = -y\), and so on for all four faces. Outflow and inflow balance.

The other side of the same lemma is uniqueness (figure 16.21). Let \(w\) be the difference of two solutions. On the section \(S\) the normal derivative is zero on the boundary. If \(|\nabla w|^2\) were \(h > 0\) at the point \(P\), by continuity it would be at least \(h/2\) on a small square \(Q\) around it, as the bar shows.

Lemma 16.19 Solvability condition and uniqueness (pogoj rešljivosti in enoličnost)

Let \(S\) be a section as in theorem 16.18 and let \(g\) be a continuous function on the boundary \(\partial S\), like the arrows of the datum. Then:

  1. If \(\psi\) is a harmonic function, twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\), with \(\partial\psi/\partial n = g\) on the boundary, then \(\oint_{\partial \mathrm{S}}g\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\). For the circle with the flux everywhere outward this is impossible.
  2. Two such functions differ by a constant. The difference \(w\) has a zero normal derivative on the boundary and \(|\nabla w|^2\) is zero everywhere.
  3. The torsion datum \(g = z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\) satisfies \(\oint_{\partial \mathrm{S}}g\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\) for every section. On the rectangle the arrows outward and inward balance.
Idea

The flux of the field \(\nabla\psi\) through the boundary is the integral of its divergence, which is \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\). For uniqueness we use energy, as for the uniqueness of the boundary value problem. In the figure the flux of the circle shows it: there is no sink, so there is no solution.

Proof
  1. The field \(\vek v = \nabla\psi = (\psi_{\mathrm{y}}, \psi_{\mathrm{z}})\) is continuously differentiable and has the divergence \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\). By lemma 16.17, \(0 = \oint(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \psi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = \oint g\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  2. Let \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_2\) be two such functions and \(w = \psi_1 - \psi_2\). Then \(\nabla^2w = 0\) and \(\partial w/\partial n = 0\) on the boundary. The field \(w\nabla w\) has the divergence \(|\nabla w|^2 + w\nabla^2w = |\nabla w|^2\), and by lemma 16.17, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint w\,\partial w/\partial n\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\). The function \(|\nabla w|^2\) is continuous and nonnegative, so it is zero everywhere. Indeed, if it were equal to \(h > 0\) at an interior point \(P\), then by continuity it would be at least \(h/2\) on a small square \(Q\) around \(P\) that lies in \(S\), and by monotonicity (lemma 4.32, points 2 and 6) the integral would be at least \(h/2\) times the area of the square \(Q\), so greater than zero. On the boundary it is zero by continuity. So \(\nabla w = 0\). The function \((x, y, z) \mapsto w(y, z)\) then has zero partial derivatives on the prism \((0, \ell) \times\) interior of \(S\). This is a connected open set (definition 1.136), since a broken line in the connected interior of \(S\) is completed with a segment along the axis \(x\). By lemma 1.139, \(w\) is constant on the interior of \(S\), and by continuity on all of \(S\). In the figure this is the square \(Q\) around the point \(P\), where \(|\nabla w|^2\) is at least \(h/2\).
  3. The field \(\vek v = (z, -y)\) has the divergence \(\partial z/\partial y + \partial(-y)/\partial z = 0\), and by lemma 16.17, \(0 = \oint(z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s\).
Explanation

Point 3 says that the condition demanded by point 1 always holds in torsion, and so there is no contradiction. The condition is necessary. That it is also sufficient, that is, that a solution exists for every such section, we do not prove here. SADD places such problems in potential theory (section 9.3.2, PDF p. 252). For the sections of this chapter we find the solution: the circle (\(\psi = 0\)), the ellipse (section 16.3) and the rectangle with a series (section 16.5). The constant that point 2 leaves is the displacement along the axis \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha c\) of all points of the section together, a rigid displacement. In the rectangle the flux through the boundary is zero, as the balance of the arrows outward and inward shows, in the circle it is not.

Example for the condition: for a circle with the radius \(20\) mm and the datum \(g = 10\) mm, \(\oint g\,\mathrm{d}s = 1256{,}6\) mm\(^2 \ne 0\), so there is no solution. The rectangle \(20 \times 40\) mm gives four faces with \(\int g\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\) each: \(\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}z\,\mathrm{d}z = 0\) on \(y = \pm a\) and \(\int_{-\mathrm{a}}^{a}y\,\mathrm{d}y = 0\) on \(z = \pm b\). At a corner \(g\) has two values, \(z = 20\) mm on the face \(y = a\) and \(-y = -10\) mm on the face \(z = b\), because there are two normals there. The datum is thus not continuous at the corners, and the rectangle demands more care (section 16.5). In the figure this is the circle with its flux and the rectangle with balanced arrows.

Example for guessing: for the strip, \(\psi = 0\) gives \(\partial\psi/\partial n = 0\), and on the face \(y = a\) the amount \(z\) is missing, that is \(20\) mm at the corner, \(10\) mm at \(z = 10\) mm and \(0\) at \(z = 0\). The function \(\psi = 0{,}6\,yz\) of the ellipse gives \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = 0{,}6z\) and \(0{,}4z\) is missing, that is \(8{,}0\) mm at the corner. Neither of them is thus the solution for the rectangle. The missing part is the difference between the datum and what \(\psi\) gives.

Source: The proof by the divergence lemma is ours, not from the source. SADD section 9.3.2 (PDF p. 252) states that such boundary problems belong to potential theory (Kellogg 1969). The numbers are ours (num-02.py).

What does the warping do to the torsion constant? The expression (16.24) has the terms \(y\psi_{\mathrm{z}} - z\psi_{\mathrm{y}}\) of unknown sign, so we do not know whether \(J\) is larger or smaller than \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) and whether it is positive at all. The answer is one equation, shown by figure 16.22: the warping removes a part of the polar moment, what remains is the torsion constant.

Let us draw what the lemma says. At the top is the strip \(20 \times 40\) mm: the long bar is \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 133\,333\) mm\(^4\). Below it the same length is divided into the \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\) and the \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2 = 60\,155\) mm\(^4\), the part that the warping removes. At the bottom is the square \(20 \times 20\) mm with the same division: the removal is smaller, \(J/I_{\mathrm{p}} = 0.8435\).

Lemma 16.20 The torsion constant is smaller than the polar moment (torzijska konstanta je manjša od polarnega momenta)

Let \(\psi\) be the warping function of the section \(S\) as in theorem 16.18, satisfying (16.23). Let \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = \int_{\mathrm{S}} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A\) be the polar second moment of area of the section about \(O\), as in lemma 16.2. Then, as figure 16.22 shows: \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) is the long bar, \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2\) is the removal, \(J\) is what remains.

  1. \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}} - \int_{\mathrm{S}} |\nabla\psi|^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), so \(J \le I_{\mathrm{p}}\). In the figure this is the bar \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) without the removed part.
  2. \(J = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \big( (\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z)^2 + (\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y)^2 \big)\,\mathrm{d}A > 0\). The bar \(J\) always has a positive length.
  3. \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\) exactly when \(\psi\) is constant. Then the removal is zero and the bars \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(J\) are equal.
Idea

The term with \(\psi\) in \(J\) we turn with the divergence theorem in the plane into an integral over the boundary, where the boundary condition links it to the energy \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2\). The removed part is \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2\) in the figure.

Proof
  1. The field \(\vek v = (-z\,\psi,\ y\,\psi)\) has the divergence \(-z\psi_{\mathrm{y}} + y\psi_{\mathrm{z}}\). By lemma 16.17, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}(y\psi_{\mathrm{z}} - z\psi_{\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint\psi\,(-z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + y\,n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = -\oint\psi\,\partial\psi/\partial n\,\mathrm{d}s\) by the boundary condition.
  2. The field \(\psi\nabla\psi\) has the divergence \(|\nabla\psi|^2 + \psi\nabla^2\psi = |\nabla\psi|^2\), so \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla\psi|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint\psi\,\partial\psi/\partial n\,\mathrm{d}s\). From step 1, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}(y\psi_{\mathrm{z}} - z\psi_{\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}A = -\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla\psi|^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), and in the expression for \(J\) from equation (16.24) point 1 follows.
  3. Expand the squares: \((\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z)^2 + (\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y)^2 = |\nabla\psi|^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 2\,(y\psi_{\mathrm{z}} - z\psi_{\mathrm{y}})\). By step 2 the integral is \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2 + I_{\mathrm{p}} - 2\int|\nabla\psi|^2 = I_{\mathrm{p}} - \int|\nabla\psi|^2 = J\), which is the equality of point 2.
  4. Positivity in point 2: if \(J = 0\), the continuous nonnegative function under the integral would be zero everywhere (as in step 2 of the proof of lemma 16.19), so \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = z\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = -y\). The mixed derivatives would be \(\psi_{\mathrm{yz}} = 1\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{zy}} = -1\), which by theorem 1.131 is not possible for a twice continuously differentiable \(\psi\). So \(J > 0\). That would mean that the shear angle is zero everywhere.
  5. Point 3: by point 1, \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\) exactly when \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2 = 0\). As in step 2 of the proof of lemma 16.19, then \(\nabla\psi = 0\) and \(\psi\) is constant on the interior of \(S\), and by continuity on all of \(S\). Conversely, for constant \(\psi\) the integral is zero. In the figure this is the case where the removal is zero.
Explanation

Result 2 says that \(J\) is the integral of a sum of squares of shear strains, \((\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + \gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}^2)/\alpha^2\) by lemma 16.16. This sum, multiplied by \(G/2\), is the strain energy density (definition 3.59 with Hooke's law \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = G\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\)), so \(J\) cannot be negative. Result 1 says that warping subtracts \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2 \ge 0\) from \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\). Warping thus always reduces the stiffness: plane sections (\(\psi = 0\)) give \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}}\) and therefore always overestimate the stiffness. For the strip \(20 \times 40\) mm, \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2 = 60\,155\) mm\(^4\), which is \(0{,}4512\) of \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 133\,333\) mm\(^4\), and \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\), the ratio \(J/I_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}5488\). For the square \(20 \times 20\) mm, \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2 = 4174\) mm\(^4\), \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 26\,667\) mm\(^4\) and \(J = 22\,492\) mm\(^4\), the ratio \(0{,}8435\): the square bulges less than the strip. The strip and the square have corners, so the lemma is not proved for them here (explanation of theorem 16.18). The numbers confirm it all the same: we computed \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2\) directly from the series for \(\psi\), and \(J\) with the series for \(J\) of section 16.5, and the difference \(I_{\mathrm{p}} - J\) agrees with \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2\) to the last digit given, \(60\,155\) and \(4174\) mm\(^4\) (num-02.py). For the ellipse with the semi-axes \(10\) and \(20\) mm, \(\psi = k\,yz\) with \(k = 0{,}6\), and \(\int|\nabla\psi|^2 = k^2\int(y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A = k^2I_{\mathrm{p}}\), so \(J = (1 - k^2)I_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}640\,I_{\mathrm{p}} = 50\,265\) mm\(^4\) (derived in section 16.3).

The origin \(O\) does not matter. Let us move it by \((y_0, z_0)\) and denote the coordinates from the new origin by \(\bar y = y - y_0\), \(\bar z = z - z_0\). The function \(\bar\psi = \psi - z_0\,y + y_0\,z\) is harmonic, because the added function is linear, its normal derivative is \(\partial\psi/\partial n - z_0n_{\mathrm{y}} + y_0n_{\mathrm{z}} = \bar z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - \bar y\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\), which is the boundary condition for the new coordinates. At the same time \(\bar\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - \bar z = \psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z\) and \(\bar\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + \bar y = \psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y\), so the stresses are the same, and by point 2 so is \(J\). For the strip moved by \(3\) mm and \(-4\) mm, at the point \((5, 7)\) mm the ratio \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/(G\alpha) = -1{,}3228\) mm before and after the move, \(J\) is \(73\,178\) mm\(^4\) in both cases, and the polar moment about a point \(5\) mm from the centroid is \(153\,333\) mm\(^4\) instead of \(133\,333\) mm\(^4\), which is \(I_{\mathrm{p}} + A\,d^2\). The number \(J\) thus does not change, and \(I_{\mathrm{p}}\) depends on the center. The warping function is thus determined up to an added linear function (a shift of the center of twist) and a constant (lemma 16.19, a rigid displacement along the axis). Figure 16.23 shows the new origin and the point where the stress vector does not change.

Source: We do not find the equation \(J = I_{\mathrm{p}} - \int|\nabla\psi|^2\) and the positivity in SADD (9.3.24), where \(J\) is given only as an integral. The proof by energy is ours. The numbers are from num-02.py.

Let us draw the shift of the center of twist (figure 16.23). On the left is the strip with the original origin \(O\) and the new origin at the point \((y_0, z_0) = (3, -4)\) mm, the shift is the vector between them. At the point \((5, 7)\) mm the vector \((\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z, \psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y)\) is the same for both origins, so \(J\) is the same too. On the right is the annulus with its center at the new origin: the displacement along the axis \(\alpha\psi\) is there a tilted line, because \(\psi\) is affine, and the section stays plane.

When is the warping zero? The answer is given by point 3 of the lemma and by a conclusion that chapter 13 used without proof. The answer is in the figure: the annulus has a center from which every point of its boundary is equally far.

Let us draw the boundaries for which the warping is zero (figure 16.24). In the figure is the annulus with two circles about the center \(O\). On a circle the normal \(\vek n\) is parallel to the radius and the tangent is perpendicular to it, so the distance \(r\) from \(O\) does not change along the tangent. Two arcs that meet at the junction have the same \(r\) there and lie on the same circle.

Corollary 16.21 Sections stay plane exactly for circles and annuli (ravni prerezi natanko pri krogu in kolobarju)

Let \(S\) be a section as in theorem 16.18. Then for the annulus and the strip:

  1. The warping function is constant exactly when every connected part of the boundary is a circle with the center at \(O\). This is a circle with its center at \(O\).
  2. The warping function is affine, \(\psi = c + p\,y + q\,z\) with constants \(c\), \(p\), \(q\), exactly when every connected part of the boundary is a circle with the same center. Then the displacement along the axis \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha\psi\) is an affine function of the place in the section, and the section stays plane, it only tilts. In the figure this is the annulus with its tilted line.

So the sections stay plane for the circle and for the annulus bounded by two circles with the same center, and for no other boundary. If the center is at \(O\), then \(\psi = 0\). Such is the annulus in the figure.

Proof
  1. Let \(\psi\) be constant. Then \(\partial\psi/\partial n = 0\) and the boundary condition (16.23) gives \(z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) on the boundary. The tangent of the boundary is \(\vek t = (-n_{\mathrm{z}}, n_{\mathrm{y}})\) and the derivative of \(r^2 = y^2 + z^2\) along it is \(2\,(y\,t_{\mathrm{y}} + z\,t_{\mathrm{z}}) = 2\,(-y\,n_{\mathrm{z}} + z\,n_{\mathrm{y}}) = 0\). The distance \(r\) from \(O\) is thus constant along every connected smooth curve of the boundary. In the figure this is the tangent, along which \(r\) is constant.
  2. Smooth arcs of the boundary that meet have the same \(r\) at the junction, so they lie on the same circle about \(O\). A closed curve that lies on a circle is the whole circle. Every connected part of the boundary is thus a circle about \(O\). In the figure these are the arcs at the junction.
  3. Conversely, let the boundary be made of circles about \(O\). The normal there is parallel to the position vector \((y, z)\), so \(z\,n_{\mathrm{y}} - y\,n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), and the function \(\psi = 0\) satisfies \(\nabla^2\psi = 0\) and the boundary condition. By lemma 16.19, point 2, it is the only solution up to a constant. Steps 1 to 3 prove point 1. In the figure the normal is parallel to the radius.
  4. For point 2 we move the center of twist to the point \((y_0, z_0)\). The function \(\bar\psi = \psi - z_0\,y + y_0\,z\) is harmonic and satisfies the boundary condition (16.23) for the coordinates \(\bar y = y - y_0\), \(\bar z = z - z_0\) (computed in the explanation of lemma 16.20). Let \(\psi = c + p\,y + q\,z\). With \(z_0 = p\) and \(y_0 = -q\), \(\bar\psi = c\) is constant, and by point 1 for the new center every connected part of the boundary is a circle with the center \((-q, p)\). The center of twist is shifted in the figure.
  5. Conversely, let every connected part of the boundary be a circle with the center \((y_0, z_0)\). By point 1 for this center, \(\bar\psi\) is constant, \(\bar\psi = c\). Then \(\psi = c + z_0\,y - y_0\,z\) is a warping function for \(O\) that is affine, and by lemma 16.19, point 2, every other one differs from it only by a constant. This is the annulus with its center at the new origin.
Explanation

The circle and the annulus thus do not bulge because for them the right-hand side of the boundary condition for \(\partial\psi/\partial n\) is zero. This is the proof of the claim of chapter 13 that the circle does not warp because of axial symmetry: there the symmetry was the argument, here it is a conclusion from the equation. For every other boundary, for example the strip of section 16.1, \(\psi\) is not affine and the section bulges: for \(20 \times 40\) mm the largest displacement along the axis is only \(0{,}953\) \(\mu\)m at \(50\) N m, but the warping nevertheless reduces the stiffness to \(J = 0{,}549\,I_{\mathrm{p}}\). The strip in the figure has straight sides, not circles.

Source: The proof is ours. SADD section 9.3 (PDF p. 246) says that circular sections stay plane because of symmetry, and the same conclusion for every section with a different boundary makes the warping unavoidable.

The task is thus: find a harmonic function \(\psi\) with a known normal derivative on the boundary and from it compute \(J\) and the stresses. For the circle the solution is \(\psi = 0\). For other shapes the form with a normal derivative is awkward: the boundary condition is not a value of the function but its derivative. The next section therefore looks for another function, one that is constant on the boundary and from which we read the stresses directly.

16.3 Prandtl's function

In section 16.2 we led the twisting of a prism to the warping function \(\psi(y, z)\), harmonic in the cross section \(S\) with a boundary condition on its derivative (theorem 16.18). What interests us above all is where in the section the stresses are large and how large a moment it carries. Is there a function from which the stresses can be read directly, and which has a simpler condition on the boundary than \(\psi\)? Such a condition would be the value of the function on the boundary, not its derivative. We shall call this function Prandtl's and use it in this section to solve the ellipse, the equilateral triangle and, once more, the circle.

We take the stresses from section 16.2. For small twists and Hooke's law (theorem 3.19), by lemma 16.16 only two shear stresses are nonzero. They are expressed with the shear modulus \(G\) (definition 3.17), the twist per unit length \(\alpha\) and the warping function:

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z) , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y) , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0 . \tag{16.25}\]

Here \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}}\) mean the partial derivatives \(\partial\psi/\partial y\) and \(\partial\psi/\partial z\). No stress depends on \(x\), so the equilibrium equation in the direction \(x\) (theorem 2.31, without body force) remains the only one:

\[\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial z} = 0 . \tag{16.26}\]

This equation connects only two stresses. We shall find one function that carries both of them, as in section 4.7.8 we looked for a function from its derivatives. But first let us see what the free lateral surface demands of the stresses.

Take the section \(S\) and draw it together with the axes \(y\) and \(z\) [figure 16.25]. The outline of the section is the curve that bounds it, and we call it the boundary. On the boundary we choose a point \(P\). In it the outward normal \(\vek n\) is the unit vector \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) that points out of the section and is perpendicular to the boundary, and the tangent is the line that touches the boundary at \(P\). Next to the point \(P\) a small piece of material lies on the lateral surface of the prism. The surface carries no load, since it is free (definition 16.1), so the stress vector on it is zero. By Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.26) the component of this vector in the direction of the bar's axis, for the normal \((0, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) of the lateral surface, equals \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}}\), and therefore

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 \quad \text{on the boundary.} \tag{16.27}\]

This is the scalar product of the pair \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\) with the normal \(\vek n\). The shear stress \(\boldsymbol\tau\) is this pair, drawn as an arrow in the plane of the section. If the scalar product is zero, it is perpendicular to \(\vek n\), so it lies along the tangent. An oblique arrow would have a component along the normal, and the force in the direction of the bar's axis would then have to be carried by a lateral surface that holds nothing. Such stresses do not exist on a free boundary: the shear stress on the boundary is always tangent to the boundary.

The equilibrium equation (16.26) and the boundary condition (16.27) speak of both stresses together. Let \(\Phi\) be a function whose derivatives are the stresses. If \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}\), the left side of equation (16.26) equals \(\Phi_{\mathrm{zy}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{yz}}\), which is zero because the mixed derivatives of a smooth function are equal. Equilibrium is then satisfied by itself, and the boundary condition becomes simple: the tangent to the boundary has the direction \(\vek t = (-n_{\mathrm{z}}, n_{\mathrm{y}})\) (the normal turned by a right angle counterclockwise), so the derivative of \(\Phi\) along the boundary is \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} t_{\mathrm{y}} + \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} t_{\mathrm{z}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\), which by equation (16.27) is zero. The function \(\Phi\) does not change its value along the boundary.

How do we picture \(\Phi\)? As the height of a hill above the section, with height zero at the boundary (figure 16.36, explained in detail for the ellipse). The stress at each point runs along the line of constant height, just as a path along a contour line of a map stays at the same height, and it is larger the steeper the hill is there, since its length equals the slope, that is the length of the gradient. Where the hill is flat the stress is small, where it is steep it is large. How much moment the section carries can therefore be read from the volume of the hill, as follows.

Definition 16.22 Prandtl stress function (Prandtlova funkcija)

Let \(S\) be the section of a prism in Saint-Venant torsion (definition 16.1) with the stresses (16.25). A function \(\Phi : S \to \mathbb{R}\) with values in N/mm, twice continuously differentiable in the interior of the section, is the Prandtl stress function (Prandtlova funkcija) of the torsion if at every point of the section

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial y} . \tag{16.28}\]

The function assigns one number to every point of the section. Its values are a stress multiplied by a length, so we measure them in N/mm.

Explanation

It is named after Prandtl, who in 1903 showed that the same equations hold for it as for a membrane under pressure (section 16.4). It is called a stress function because the stresses are obtained by differentiation. The letter \(\Phi\) has several meanings in the book: \(\varphi\) is the rotation of a section (chapter 13) and Airy's function (chapter 11), and the capital \(\Phi\) is a local name for a mapping in the proofs of chapter 4 and in section 16.1. SADD writes \(\phi\) for Prandtl's function. From here on, \(\Phi\) in this chapter means only this function.

Source: SADD section 9.3.1, equation (9.3.8) (PDF p. 248), the name after Prandtl and the year 1903 in section 9.3.4 (PDF p. 254). SADD has the bar's axis \(z\), the section in the plane \(x, y\) and the twist \(\alpha\), we have the axis \(x\) and the section in the plane \(y, z\): SADD's \((x, y)\) is our \((y, z)\) and its \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\) is our \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) with the sign according to our axes.

Does such a function exist at all for the stresses (16.25)? From equilibrium it follows that it does. The theorem on a field from partial derivatives (theorem 4.115) is exactly this step: if the mixed derivatives of a pair of functions agree and the region is simply connected (definition 1.142), the pair comes from one function. A section with a hole, such as a tube, does not guarantee this. So in this section we restrict ourselves to sections without holes and leave tubes for section 16.8.

We look at the difference in a figure (figure 16.26). On the left is a section without a hole and in it a loop that we can shrink to a point without leaving the section. On the right is a tube with a hole, and a loop around the hole does not shrink, since it would have to cross the hole.

The proof of the lemma takes place in a cylinder over the section (figure 16.27). We draw the cylinder \(D\) standing over the open set \(E\), and in it the section \(S\) with its boundary, where the function will be constant. In the cylinder we take a segment along the axis \(x\), on which the function \(\varphi\) will be constant, and a loop that we shrink. At the lower right are two functions with the same derivatives that differ by a constant.

Lemma 16.23 Existence of the Prandtl function (obstoj Prandtlove funkcije)

Let \(S\) be a bounded section whose interior is connected and simply connected (definition 1.142) and whose boundary is one closed curve with a piecewise continuously differentiable tangent, let the warping function \(\psi\) of theorem 16.18 be twice continuously differentiable on an open set \(E\) that contains \(S\) and is connected (definition 1.136) and simply connected (for the circle, the ellipse and the triangle \(\psi\) is a polynomial and \(E\) is the whole plane, for the rectangle see section 16.5), and let \(G\alpha \ne 0\). Then:

  1. A Prandtl function \(\Phi\) of the section exists (definition 16.22), twice continuously differentiable on \(E\).
  2. The function \(\Phi\) is determined up to an added constant, and it has a constant value on the boundary.
  3. Since the stresses contain only derivatives, we can choose \(\Phi = 0\) on the boundary.
Idea

We show that the field \((0, -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\) satisfies the condition of the theorem on a field from derivatives, because that condition is equilibrium (16.26). Constancy on the boundary is an expression of the boundary condition (16.27).

Proof
  1. Let \(D = E \times \mathbb{R}\) be the cylinder over the set \(E\). It is an open and connected set. It is also simply connected: a loop in \(D\) is contracted by contracting its projection into \(E\) by definition 1.142 and at the same time pulling the coordinate \(x\) to a constant value.
  2. The field \(\vek w = (0, -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\) is continuously differentiable on the cylinder \(D\), since the stresses (16.25) have continuous first derivatives (\(\psi\) has continuous second ones). Because it does not depend on \(x\), the derivatives with respect to \(x\) are zero. The condition of theorem 4.115 is the equality of mixed derivatives, \(\partial w_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial z = \partial w_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial y\), and the other pairs are zero. The first two are \(-\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial z\) and \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial y\) and they are equal exactly by equation (16.26). By the theorem a continuously differentiable function \(\varphi\) exists on \(D\) with \(\partial\varphi/\partial y = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\partial\varphi/\partial z = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\partial\varphi/\partial x = 0\).
  3. The derivative with respect to \(x\) is zero on every segment along the axis \(x\) in \(D\), so by corollary 1.86 \(\varphi\) is constant along it and is a function of \((y, z)\) only. We call it \(\Phi\). Since the first derivatives \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are continuously differentiable on \(E\), \(\Phi\) is twice continuously differentiable on \(E\), and so also at the points of the boundary of the section. Equation (16.28) holds.
  4. If \(\tilde\Phi\) is another such function on \(E\), the difference \(\tilde\Phi - \Phi\) has both derivatives zero on the connected set \(E\), so it is constant.
  5. On the boundary, by what was written before the definition, \(\Phi\) has the derivative along the tangent \(\vek t\) equal to \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} t_{\mathrm{y}} + \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} t_{\mathrm{z}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) by equation (16.27). The boundary is one connected curve, and a function with zero derivative along it is constant. Point 3 follows, because \(\Phi - \Phi_{\text{boundary}}\) gives the same stresses.

Source: SADD section 9.3.1 (PDF p. 248-249): at (9.3.8) and (9.3.12) it says that the function is constant on the boundary and that the constant is chosen to be zero. The proof of existence with the theorem on a field from derivatives is not from the source. The existence of the warping function for a general section is stated by SADD and we do not prove it (section 16.2).

What equation does \(\Phi\) satisfy in the interior? Equilibrium is already used up. What remains is a requirement that the warping function satisfies by itself, but \(\Phi\) must be given it: the shear strains must come from one displacement. From equations (16.25),

\[\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial z} = G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{zy}} + 1 - \psi_{\mathrm{yz}} + 1) = 2G\alpha , \tag{16.29}\]

since the mixed derivatives of \(\psi\) are equal. The left side does not contain \(\psi\), so this is a condition on the stresses themselves. We call it the compatibility condition (pogoj kompatibilnosti) of torsion, since like the compatibility equations (theorem 1.133) it ensures that the strains come from one displacement. Written with \(\Phi\) it is the equation of the theorem that follows.

What does equation (16.29) say, shown on a figure? Around a small square of the section in the axes \(y\) and \(z\) [figure 16.28] we go round the loop and add the stress along the sides. On the lower and left side the stress has the value at the corner, on the upper and right side it differs by the derivative times the side length, on the upper one with the opposite sign because the circuit runs against the axis \(y\) there. So the sum does not cancel, and what remains is the difference of derivatives times the area. The equation therefore says: the circulation of the stress around every small square is \(2G\alpha\,\Delta A\), the same everywhere, since it is twice the rotation rate \(\alpha\) of the material, multiplied by \(G\). If \(\Phi\) did not satisfy this, the strains would not come from one displacement.

We look at the moment in a figure (figure 16.29). At a point of the section two components of the shear stress act, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) along \(y\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) along \(z\). Their arms about the axis \(x\) are \(z\) and \(y\). The position vector \((y, z)\) points from the axis to the point, and the gradient \(\nabla\Phi\) points toward the top of the hill, perpendicular to the stress.

How do we compute from \(\Phi\) the moment that the section carries? The moment is the sum of the moments of the shear forces of the section about the axis \(x\). The force \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) at the point \((y, z)\) has the arm \(y\) and the force \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) the arm \(z\) with the opposite sign, so

\[M_{\mathrm{x}} = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \big( y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} - z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}A = -\int_{\mathrm{S}} \big( y\,\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\,\Phi_{\mathrm{z}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{16.30}\]

The expression \(y\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) is the scalar product of the position vector \((y, z)\) with the gradient \(\nabla\Phi = (\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\). This product is a part of the divergence of the field \(\Phi\,(y, z)\). The divergence theorem (theorem 4.14, section 4.2.5) turns the divergence into an integral over the boundary, where \(\Phi = 0\). Since the section is a figure in the plane, we need the theorem in the plane, lemma 16.17, which we proved in section 16.2.

Why is the moment exactly twice the volume? Cut the hill into thin layers between heights \(h\) and \(h + \mathrm{d}h\) (figure 16.36). A layer is a strip around the level line of height \(h\), which encloses the area \(A(h)\). The strip has width \(\mathrm{d}n\), the stress in it is tangent and of size \(\mathrm{d}h/\mathrm{d}n\) (the slope of the hill), so the force on a piece of the strip of length \(\mathrm{d}s\) is \((\mathrm{d}h/\mathrm{d}n)\,\mathrm{d}n\,\mathrm{d}s = \mathrm{d}h\,\mathrm{d}s\). Its moment about the axis is \(\mathrm{d}h\) times the arm \(r_\perp\,\mathrm{d}s\), and the sum around the closed level line is \(\mathrm{d}h\oint r_\perp\,\mathrm{d}s = 2A(h)\,\mathrm{d}h\), because \(r_\perp\,\mathrm{d}s\) is twice the area of the narrow wedge from the axis to the piece of line. Adding all layers gives \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\int_0^{\Phi_{\max}}A(h)\,\mathrm{d}h\), and \(\int A(h)\,\mathrm{d}h\) is the volume under the hill. The factor 2 is thus twice the wedge area, not a computational extra. The same result without the divergence follows in the theorem.

Now we have everything for the theorem. It contains three claims: the equation for \(\Phi\), the moment, and a converse which says that every solution of the equation really is a torsion.

For the proof we look at a figure (figure 16.30). On the left is the section \(S\) and in it a vertical strip, on the right the height of the hill \(\Phi\) along the strip, the profile. At the ends of the strip the section is at its boundary and \(\Phi = 0\), so the sum of increments along the strip is zero. At the top the profile curves downward: the curvature \(\Phi_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is negative, and together with \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}}\) the sum equals \(-2G\alpha\).

Theorem 16.24 Prandtl's equation (Prandtlova enačba)

Let \(S\) be a section as in lemma 16.23, and let \(\Phi\) be the Prandtl function of the section with the value zero on the boundary, twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\) (for a rectangle this does not happen at the corners, section 16.5).

  1. The curvature of the hill is the same everywhere:
    \[\nabla^2\Phi = \frac{\partial^2\Phi}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2\Phi}{\partial z^2} = -2G\alpha \quad \text{in } S , \qquad \Phi = 0 \quad \text{on } \partial S . \tag{16.31}\]
  2. The resultant of the forces of the section is zero, and its moment about the axis \(x\) is twice the volume under the hill:
    \[M_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}} \Phi\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{16.32}\]
    So \(J = (2/G\alpha)\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\) is the torsion constant of theorem 16.18, \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = GJ\alpha\).
  3. Conversely, let \(\Phi\) be a twice continuously differentiable function with the properties (16.31). Then the field (16.28) satisfies equilibrium and the free lateral surface, and a warping function \(\psi\) exists (harmonic, with the boundary condition of theorem 16.18) that gives the same stresses.
Idea

The first claim is the compatibility condition (16.29), written with \(\Phi\). The second is the divergence theorem in the section, because the boundary term cancels owing to \(\Phi = 0\). The converse goes by the same theorem on a field from derivatives, this time for \(\psi\).

Proof
  1. From equation (16.28), \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial y = -\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial z = \Phi_{\mathrm{zz}}\). The left side of equation (16.29) is therefore \(-\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nabla^2\Phi\) and equals \(2G\alpha\). The boundary condition is point 3 of lemma 16.23.
  2. The force in the direction \(y\): \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\,\mathrm{d}A\). By lemma 16.17 with the field \(\vek v = (0, \Phi)\) this is \(\oint\Phi n_{\mathrm{z}}\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\), because \(\Phi = 0\) on the boundary. Similarly with the field \((\Phi, 0)\) for the force in the direction \(z\): \(-\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}\,\mathrm{d}A = -\oint\Phi n_{\mathrm{y}}\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\). There are no normal stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), so there is no force in the direction \(x\). Since the shear resultants are zero too, the moments about \(y\) and \(z\) are zero as well (as in step 5 of the proof of theorem 16.18).
  3. The field \(\vek v = (y\,\Phi, z\,\Phi)\) has the divergence \(\Phi + y\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + \Phi + z\Phi_{\mathrm{z}} = 2\Phi + y\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\). By lemma 16.17, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}(2\Phi + y\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint\Phi\,(y\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + z\,n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\), since \(\Phi = 0\) on the boundary.
  4. By equation (16.30), \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = -\int_{\mathrm{S}}(y\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} + z\Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}A = 2\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\). The same moment for \(\psi\) equals \(GJ\alpha\) (theorem 16.18), whence \(J\).
  5. The converse. Let \(\Phi\) be as in point 3 of the theorem. The field \(\vek w = (0, -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}) = (0, \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\) is by construction the gradient of the function \(\Phi\), so equilibrium (16.26) is satisfied (mixed derivatives of \(\Phi\)). The derivative of \(\Phi\) along the boundary is zero, because \(\Phi = 0\) on the boundary. This derivative is \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{y}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}n_{\mathrm{z}}\), so (16.27) holds.
  6. We look for \(\psi\) with \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}/(G\alpha) + z\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}/(G\alpha) - y\) (equations (16.25) rewritten). The mixed derivatives: \(\partial_{\mathrm{z}}\psi_{\mathrm{y}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{zz}}/(G\alpha) + 1\) and \(\partial_{\mathrm{y}}\psi_{\mathrm{z}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}}/(G\alpha) - 1\). They are equal exactly when \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} + \Phi_{\mathrm{zz}} = -2G\alpha\), which holds. By theorem 4.115 (as in lemma 16.23) \(\psi\) therefore exists. For \(\psi\) we have \(\psi_{\mathrm{yy}} + \psi_{\mathrm{zz}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{zy}}/(G\alpha) - \Phi_{\mathrm{yz}}/(G\alpha) = 0\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + \psi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}} = (\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{y}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{z}})/(G\alpha) + zn_{\mathrm{y}} - yn_{\mathrm{z}} = zn_{\mathrm{y}} - yn_{\mathrm{z}}\), since \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{y}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{z}}\) is the derivative along the boundary and is zero.

Source: SADD section 9.3.1, (9.3.9), (9.3.12), (9.3.15)-(9.3.18) (PDF p. 248-251). The converse and the use of the theorem on a field from derivatives are not from the source.

We proved the theorem when \(\Phi\) is twice continuously differentiable up to the boundary. For the circle, the ellipse and the triangle, which we compute in this section, the solutions are polynomials and the condition holds. The rectangle has corners. Along the side \(y = a\) we have \(\Phi = 0\), so there \(\Phi_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} = -2G\alpha\), while along the side \(z = b\) we have \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\). The second derivative \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}}\) therefore has two different limits at the corner. The mixed derivative \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yz}}\) is not even bounded near the corner: the series of section 16.5 gives on the diagonal, at the distances \(0{,}1\), \(0{,}01\) and \(0{,}001\) mm from the corner, \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yz}}/(G\alpha) = 5{,}72\), \(8{,}65\) and \(11{,}58\), larger by \((4/\pi)\ln 10 = 2{,}93\) for each ten times smaller distance. So at the corner \(\Phi\) is not twice continuously differentiable, and the proof with the divergence theorem would need a cut-out near the corner and a limit. For sections with corners we do not prove it here. SADD (PDF p. 248-251) uses Green's theorem without this condition. The rectangle will be solved in section 16.5 with a series and with checked numbers.

We look at this in a figure (figure 16.31). On the left is the corner with the vertical and the horizontal side, along which \(\Phi = 0\), and the diagonal toward the corner. On the right is the graph of the mixed derivative along the diagonal: at every ten times smaller offset it grows by a constant step, so it is unbounded.

Is the solution of equation (16.31) unique? If there were several, the same torsion would have several stress fields. We show that this is not so, by energy, as in chapter 11 we proved the uniqueness of the boundary value problem.

We draw what two solutions would mean (figure 16.32). On the right are the solutions \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) along a line through the section, and since they have the same boundary, both are zero at the ends. The difference is zero there. On the left are the boundary, a disc around a point \(P\) at which the slope of the difference would be nonzero, the field \(w\,\nabla w\), which vanishes at the boundary, and a path from \(P\) to the boundary.

Lemma 16.25 Uniqueness of Prandtl's equation (enoličnost Prandtlove enačbe)

Let \(S\) be a section whose interior is connected and for which lemma 16.17 holds. Let \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) be functions, twice continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(S\), with \(\nabla^2f_1 = \nabla^2f_2 = -2G\alpha\) in \(S\) and \(f_1 = f_2 = 0\) on \(\partial S\). Then \(f_1 = f_2\).

Idea

The difference \(w = f_1 - f_2\) is harmonic and zero on the boundary. The energy \(\int|\nabla w|^2\) is then zero.

Proof
  1. Let \(w = f_1 - f_2\). Then \(\nabla^2w = 0\) in \(S\) and \(w = 0\) on the boundary.
  2. The field \(\vek v = w\,\nabla w = (w\,w_{\mathrm{y}}, w\,w_{\mathrm{z}})\) is continuously differentiable and has the divergence \(w_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + w\,\nabla^2w = |\nabla w|^2\) (product rule). By lemma 16.17, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint w\,(w_{\mathrm{y}}n_{\mathrm{y}} + w_{\mathrm{z}}n_{\mathrm{z}})\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\), since \(w = 0\) on the boundary.
  3. A continuous nonnegative function \(|\nabla w|^2\) with zero integral is zero everywhere (if it were positive at some point, it would be positive in a disc around it and the integral would be positive). So \(\nabla w = 0\).
  4. A function with zero gradient on a connected set is constant, and on the boundary \(w = 0\), so \(w = 0\).

Source: The same energy argument for the Laplace operator is in CM section 7.5.7 (PDF p. 340-342). The proof is not from the source.

The lemma means that for a given section there is at most one Prandtl function with zero on the boundary. If we find it by any means (by guessing, or by a series when it is twice continuously differentiable up to the boundary), it is the right one. For the rectangle, where this fails at the corners, see section 16.5. The stress field therefore does not depend on how we found \(\Phi\). The displacement field too is by theorem 11.4 unique with it, up to a rigid motion.

Let us try this on the ellipse, where \(\Phi\) can be guessed. Let the section have the semi-axis \(a\) along \(y\) and \(b\) along \(z\). The boundary is the curve \(y^2/a^2 + z^2/b^2 = 1\), and the function \(1 - y^2/a^2 - z^2/b^2\) is zero on it and positive in the interior. Take \(\Phi = c\,(1 - y^2/a^2 - z^2/b^2)\) with a constant \(c\). The boundary has the value zero for every \(c\), and we choose \(c\) so that \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\). Let us first draw this function [figure 16.33]. Above the boundary of the section we draw the profile along the axis \(y\), a parabola that falls from the top to zero at \(y = \pm a\), and the profile along the axis \(z\), which falls to zero at \(z = \pm b\). The height \(c\) is the top of the hill.

The volume under the hill is written in the theorem as \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A\). We can compute it by the change of variables theorem (theorem 4.59): we write a point of the section as \((y, z) = (a\,u,\ b\,v)\), where \((u, v)\) lies in the disc \(K\) of radius \(1\) centred at the origin. This linear mapping stretches the disc by the factor \(a\) along \(y\) and by the factor \(b\) along \(z\), so it maps it onto the ellipse, and it is injective on the whole plane. Its Jacobian determinant is constant, \(a\,b\): every piece of the disc is mapped into a piece of the ellipse with an \(ab\) times larger area.

We draw the mapping (figure 16.34). On the left is the disc \(K\) of radius \(1\). On the right is the ellipse \(S\) onto which it is mapped: along \(y\) we stretch it by \(a\) and along \(z\) by \(b\). A small piece of the disc goes into a piece of the ellipse with an \(ab\) times larger area. On the ellipse there is also the point \((a, 0)\), where the stress will be largest, and an inner ellipse on which \(\Phi\) is constant.

Theorem 16.26 Torsion of an ellipse (torzija elipse)

Let the section be an ellipse with semi-axes \(a\) along the axis \(y\) and \(b\) along the axis \(z\), \(a \le b\), and let \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) be the moment.

  1. The Prandtl function of the ellipse with zero on the boundary is
    \[\Phi = G\alpha\,\frac{a^2b^2}{a^2 + b^2}\Big( 1 - \frac{y^2}{a^2} - \frac{z^2}{b^2} \Big) . \tag{16.33}\]
  2. From the volume of the hill we get the torsion constant:
    \[J = \frac{\pi\,a^3b^3}{a^2 + b^2} , \qquad \alpha = \frac{M_{\mathrm{x}}}{GJ} . \tag{16.34}\]
  3. The stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -2M_{\mathrm{x}} z/(\pi a b^3)\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2M_{\mathrm{x}} y/(\pi a^3 b)\), the largest is at the ends of the shorter axis and equals
    \[\tau_{\max} = \frac{2M_{\mathrm{x}}}{\pi\,a^2b} . \tag{16.35}\]
  4. The warping function is \(\psi = k\,yz\) with \(k = (b^2 - a^2)/(a^2 + b^2)\).
  5. For \(a = b = R\) this agrees with the circle: \(J = \pi R^4/2\) and \(\tau = M_{\mathrm{x}}r/I_{\mathrm{p}}\).
Idea

The function is a polynomial, so it has a constant Laplace operator and zero on the boundary. The constant \(c\) is chosen from the Laplace value, \(J\) from the moment, the stresses from the derivatives. By lemma 16.25 this is the only solution.

Proof
  1. Let \(\Phi = c\,(1 - y^2/a^2 - z^2/b^2)\). On the boundary \(\Phi = 0\). The second derivatives are \(\Phi_{\mathrm{yy}} = -2c/a^2\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{zz}} = -2c/b^2\), so \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2c\,(a^2 + b^2)/(a^2b^2)\). The condition \(\nabla^2\Phi = -2G\alpha\) gives \(c = G\alpha\,a^2b^2/(a^2 + b^2)\). This is equation (16.33). By lemma 16.25 this is the function of the ellipse, and by theorem 16.24 (point 3) it belongs to a torsion of the section.
  2. We compute the integrals over the ellipse with the mapping \((u, v) \mapsto (au, bv)\) of the introduction and with lemma 16.2 for the disc \(K\) of radius \(R = 1\). The area: \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\mathrm{d}A = ab\int_{\mathrm{K}}\mathrm{d}A = \pi ab\), since \(K\) has the area \(\pi\) (the proof of lemma 16.2 with the function \(1\) in place of \(r^2\), where \(\int_0^1 r\,\mathrm{d}r = 1/2\)). The term \(y^2 = a^2u^2\) gives \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}y^2\,\mathrm{d}A = a^3b\int_{\mathrm{K}}u^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \pi a^3b/4\) and similarly \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}z^2\,\mathrm{d}A = ab^3\int_{\mathrm{K}}v^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \pi ab^3/4\).
  3. Hence \(\int_{\mathrm{S}}\Phi\,\mathrm{d}A = c\,(\pi ab - \pi ab/4 - \pi ab/4) = c\,\pi ab/2\) and by equation (16.32) \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = c\,\pi ab = G\alpha\,\pi a^3b^3/(a^2 + b^2)\). This is \(GJ\alpha\) with \(J\) from equation (16.34).
  4. From \(c = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(\pi ab)\) we get \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} = -2cz/b^2 = -2M_{\mathrm{x}}z/(\pi ab^3)\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} = 2cy/a^2 = 2M_{\mathrm{x}}y/(\pi a^3b)\). The magnitude: \(\tau^2 = (2M_{\mathrm{x}}/\pi ab)^2\,(y^2/a^4 + z^2/b^4)\).
  5. The maximum is on the boundary: with \(y = a\cos\theta\), \(z = b\sin\theta\) we have \(y^2/a^4 + z^2/b^4 = \cos^2\theta/a^2 + \sin^2\theta/b^2\), which for \(a \le b\) is largest at \(\cos^2\theta = 1\), at the point \((a, 0)\). There \(\tau = 2M_{\mathrm{x}}/(\pi ab)\cdot 1/a\), equation (16.35). An interior point has a smaller stress, since \(y^2/a^4 + z^2/b^4\) under the ellipse \(y^2/a^2 + z^2/b^2 = s^2 \le 1\) is at most \(s^2/a^2\).
  6. The warping function: from equations (16.25), \(G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z) = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} = -2G\alpha\,a^2z/(a^2 + b^2)\) and \(G\alpha\,(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y) = -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} = 2G\alpha\,b^2y/(a^2 + b^2)\). With \(\psi = k\,yz\) we have \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}} - z = (k - 1)z\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}} + y = (k + 1)y\), so \(k - 1 = -2a^2/(a^2 + b^2)\) and \(k + 1 = 2b^2/(a^2 + b^2)\), both satisfied with \(k = (b^2 - a^2)/(a^2 + b^2)\). SymPy checked them.
  7. For \(a = b = R\) we have \(k = 0\), \(J = \pi R^6/(2R^2) = \pi R^4/2\) and \(\tau^2 = (2M_{\mathrm{x}}/\pi R^2)^2\,r^2/R^4\), so \(\tau = 2M_{\mathrm{x}}r/(\pi R^4) = M_{\mathrm{x}}r/I_{\mathrm{p}}\) (lemma 16.2). This is theorem 16.3.

Source: SADD example 9.1 (PDF p. 257-258) and ONATE2 figure 4.11 (PDF p. 201): \(J = \pi a^3b^3/(a^2 + b^2)\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{i}} = 2M/(\pi a b^2)\) for ONATE's larger semi-axis \(a\) and smaller \(b\), which are our \(b\) and \(a\). SADD has the semi-axes \(a\) along \(x\) and \(b\) along \(y\) and the validity \(a > b\). The proof with the uniqueness lemma and the linear mapping of the disc is not from the source.

We draw the warping function of the ellipse (figure 16.35). On the left \(\psi = k\,yz\) has alternating signs in the quadrants, it is constant on the hyperbolas \(yz = \text{constant}\), and the displacement is largest at the boundary point at \(t = 45°\). On the right is the circle, where \(k = 0\) and \(\psi = 0\).

Example 16.27 Ellipse 10 by 20 mm (elipsa 10 × 20 mm)

For an ellipse with \(a = 10\) mm along \(y\) and \(b = 20\) mm along \(z\) and a steel bar (\(G = 75\,385\) MPa) at \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 50\) N m: \(J = 50\,265\) mm\(^4\), \(\alpha = 0{,}01320\) rad/m, \(G\alpha = 0{,}9947\) N/mm\(^3\), the top of the hill \(c = M_{\mathrm{x}}/(\pi ab) = 79{,}58\) N/mm. By equation (16.35) the largest stress is \(\tau_{\max} = 15{,}92\) MPa. The section bulges: the displacement along the bar's axis is \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha\psi = \alpha k\,yz\) with \(k = 0{,}600\) (point 4 of the theorem). On the boundary \(yz = \tfrac12 ab\sin 2t\) at the point \((a\cos t,\ b\sin t)\), so the displacement is largest at \(t = 45°\), at the point \((7{,}07;\ 14{,}14)\) mm, and there \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}792\ \mu\)m.

Let us look at where the stress flows in this ellipse [figure 16.36]. We draw the axes \(y\) and \(z\) and the boundary of the ellipse, where \(\Phi = 0\).
